paragraphs: Friend, here's the big idea. David wrote this song right after a king drove him away, and he still says, "I will bless the LORD at all times" (Psalm 34:1). He doesn't wait for the trouble to clear first. He sought the LORD, and he says the LORD answered him and "delivered me from all my fears" (Psalm 34:4). So the LORD is worth praising in the middle of the mess, not just after it.

Now, David never says the road is easy. He says "Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him from them all" (Psalm 34:19). He also says "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted" (Psalm 34:18). I think that's the part that matters most on a rough day, because the song doesn't promise a life with no trouble. It promises the LORD is near in it.

So what do you do with that, baker? David says "Taste and see that the LORD is good" (Psalm 34:8), and he doesn't say think about it for a month. Then he teaches that good days mean keeping your tongue from evil, turning away from evil, and to "seek peace and pursue it" (Psalm 34:13-14). Take refuge in Him, because David ends with this: "The LORD redeems His servants, and none who take refuge in Him will be condemned" (Psalm 34:22).
